subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then score my answer the way an AP reader would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

questions.q: In geometric optics, light is represented by rays. Which of the following best describes a light ray?
options: A line drawn along a wavefront, joining all points of the light wave that are in step
A straight line at right angles to the wavefronts, in the direction the wave moves
A thin physical beam, such as a laser's; the light from a lamp contains no such rays
A wavy line tracing the up-and-down path that the light follows as it travels
optionWhy: A student who confuses rays with wavefronts picks this. The line joining points in step is the wavefront itself; the ray crosses the wavefronts at right angles.
A ray is a model of the direction in which light travels: a straight line perpendicular to the wavefronts, pointing the way the wave is traveling. It is a drawing tool, not a physical object.
A student who thinks rays are real thin beams picks this. A ray is a line representing a direction of travel; light from a lamp can be represented by rays just as well as a laser beam can.

A student who reads the sine-curve drawing of a wave as the path of the light picks this. In one material light travels in straight lines; the sine curve is a graph of how the wave varies, not a path.
questions.explain: A ray is a model of the direction in which light travels: a straight line perpendicular to the wavefronts, pointing the way the wave is traveling. It is a drawing tool, not a physical object.

questions.q: A teacher uses a laser pointer rather than a flashlight to demonstrate how light reflects from a mirror. Which is the best reason for this choice?
options: Its light is bright enough to reach the mirror, while a flashlight's light fades out.
A flashlight's light is not made up of rays, so its path cannot be drawn.
Laser light is not a wave, so no wave effects can disturb its path.
Its narrow, single-color beam can be modeled as one ray that is easy to trace.
optionWhy: A student who thinks light travels only a limited distance, set by its brightness, picks this. A flashlight's light easily reaches a mirror across a room; it simply spreads out over a wide area.

A student who thinks a ray is a physical thin beam picks this. Light from any source can be represented by rays; a flashlight's beam needs many diverging rays, which is less convenient but not impossible.
A student who takes the ray model of a laser for the laser light itself picks this. Laser light is a wave; its wave nature, studied later, can simply be neglected in this demonstration.

A laser gives a single narrow, monochromatic beam that spreads very little, so it behaves like one ray whose path, and angles, can be seen and measured. A flashlight's wide beam also consists of light that can be represented by rays, but many of them, spreading apart.
questions.explain: A laser gives a single narrow, monochromatic beam that spreads very little, so it behaves like one ray whose path, and angles, can be seen and measured. A flashlight's wide beam also consists of light that can be represented by rays, but many of them, spreading apart.

questions.q: A student draws a ray diagram to show how light from a lamp reaches her eye after reflecting from a flat mirror. Which feature should the diagram have?
options: Arrows pointing out of her eye toward the mirror, then on to the lamp
Arrows pointing from the lamp to the mirror and then from the mirror to her eye
Rays that end at the mirror's surface, where the image of the lamp is formed and seen
Wavy lines showing the light moving up and down as it travels to the eye
optionWhy: A student who thinks seeing involves something traveling out of the eye picks this. The eye receives light; the arrows point from the source, via the mirror, into the eye.
A ray diagram shows the path of the light before and after it interacts with matter, with arrows in the direction the light travels. Light leaves the lamp, reflects at the mirror and enters the eye.

A student who thinks light travels only as far as an image on the mirror picks this. The light reflects at the mirror and continues to the eye; the diagram must show its path after the reflection too.
A student who thinks light follows a wavy path picks this. Rays are straight lines; light in air travels in straight lines between the lamp, the mirror and the eye.
questions.explain: A ray diagram shows the path of the light before and after it interacts with matter, with arrows in the direction the light travels. Light leaves the lamp, reflects at the mirror and enters the eye.

questions.q: The diagram shows circular wavefronts spreading out from a small light source S. Arrows A, B, C and D are drawn from dots on the wavefronts. Which arrow correctly represents a light ray at its point?
options: Arrow A
Arrow C
Arrow B
Arrow D
optionWhy: A student who thinks a ray runs along a wavefront picks this. Arrow A is tangent to the wavefront; a ray crosses the wavefront at 90°.

A student who thinks a small source sends all its light straight ahead, across the page to the right, as parallel rays picks this horizontal arrow. Light from a small source spreads out in all directions, so at that dot the ray points up and to the right, directly away from S.

A ray is a straight line perpendicular to the wavefront, pointing in the direction of travel. For circular wavefronts around S that direction is straight out from S, along a radius, which is how arrow B is drawn.

A student who thinks light follows a wavy path picks this. Arrow D points in the right direction, directly away from S, but a ray is a straight line; the light does not move up and down as it travels.
questions.explain: A ray is a straight line perpendicular to the wavefront, pointing in the direction of travel. For circular wavefronts around S that direction is straight out from S, along a radius, which is how arrow B is drawn.

figure.alt: A small light source S at the lower left, with three circular wavefronts drawn as arcs centered on S. Four arrows start at dots on the wavefronts. The arrow labeled A, on the outer wavefront, is straight and points along the wavefront (tangent to the arc). The arrow labeled B, on the middle wavefront, is straight and points directly away from S. The arrow labeled C, on the inner wavefront at a point up and to the right of S, is straight and points horizontally to the right. The arrow labeled D, on the middle wavefront near the bottom, points directly away from S but is drawn as a wavy line.

questions.q: A beam of light rays traveling parallel to the principal axis of a convex mirror strikes the mirror. Which statement describes the reflected rays?
options: They converge to a point in front of the mirror, where they cross.
They pass through a point behind the mirror, where they cross.
They diverge as if they came from a point behind the mirror.
They go back along their own paths, staying parallel to the axis.
optionWhy: A student who thinks every mirror focuses parallel light in front of it picks this. That is true of a concave mirror; a convex mirror's surface bulges toward the light and turns the rays away from the axis, so they never cross.

A student who thinks light actually reaches the focal point behind a convex mirror picks this. No light goes behind the mirror; the reflected rays only appear to come from that point when they are extended backward.
A convex mirror reflects rays arriving parallel to the principal axis so that they diverge; extended backward, they appear to come from a common point behind the mirror, its focal point.

A student who thinks head-on rays always reflect straight back picks this. Except at the very center, the rays strike the curved surface at an angle to the normal, so they reflect at an angle and spread apart.
questions.explain: A convex mirror reflects rays arriving parallel to the principal axis so that they diverge; extended backward, they appear to come from a common point behind the mirror, its focal point.

questions.q: Where is the focal point of a plane mirror?
options: On the mirror's surface, as a flat mirror has a focal length of zero
Infinitely far from the mirror, as parallel rays stay parallel after reflecting
Behind the mirror, as far behind it as an object is in front of it
In front of the mirror, where the rays reflected from a distant lamp cross
optionWhy: A student who equates 'no curvature' with a focal length of zero picks this. A flat mirror is the limit of a spherical mirror with an enormous radius of curvature, so f = R/2 becomes infinite, not zero.

A plane mirror reflects parallel rays as parallel rays. They never meet and never appear to come from one point at a finite distance, so the focal point is an infinite distance from the mirror (1/f = 0).

A student who thinks the image always forms at the focal point picks this. That location is where a plane mirror's image is; the focal point is a property of the mirror alone and does not depend on where any object is.

A student who thinks every mirror brings parallel rays together in front of it picks this. Light from a distant lamp arrives as parallel rays, and a plane mirror reflects them as parallel rays, which never cross.
questions.explain: A plane mirror reflects parallel rays as parallel rays. They never meet and never appear to come from one point at a finite distance, so the focal point is an infinite distance from the mirror (1/f = 0).

questions.q: A student uses 1/s_i + 1/s_o = 1/f for an object 12.0 cm in front of a convex mirror, taking s_o = +12.0 cm and f = −12.0 cm (f is positive for a concave mirror and negative for a convex mirror), and obtains s_i = −6.0 cm. What does the negative sign tell the student about the image?
options: It is inverted, standing upside down relative to the object.
It shows an error, as an image distance cannot be negative.
It is 6.0 cm behind the mirror, where light meets to form a real image.
It is 6.0 cm behind the mirror, so it is a virtual image.
optionWhy: A student who reads the sign of s_i as the image's orientation picks this. The sign of s_i gives the image's location (behind the mirror); a virtual image formed by a single mirror is in fact upright.
A student who treats s_i as an unsigned length picks this. In the mirror equation s_i is a signed location, and −6.0 cm is a valid result meaning 6.0 cm behind the mirror.
A student who thinks light actually reaches points behind a mirror picks this. No light passes behind the mirror; the rays only appear to come from 6.0 cm behind it, so the image is virtual.
In this convention a negative image distance locates the image behind the mirror. Light does not pass behind a mirror, so the reflected rays only appear to come from there: the image is virtual.
questions.explain: In this convention a negative image distance locates the image behind the mirror. Light does not pass behind a mirror, so the reflected rays only appear to come from there: the image is virtual.
questions.working: 1/s_i = 1/f − 1/s_o = −1/12.0 − 1/12.0 = −1/6.0 cm⁻¹ ⇒ s_i = −6.0 cm. In the convention in which f is positive for a concave mirror, s_i is positive for an image in front of the mirror and negative for one behind it: the image is 6.0 cm behind the mirror. No light passes behind a mirror, so the image is virtual.

questions.q: A convex mirror in a store shows images of customers standing at various distances in front of it. How does the height of each customer's image compare with the customer's height?
options: It is larger, as a convex mirror magnifies, like a magnifying glass.
It is smaller, whatever the customer's distance from the mirror.
It is equal, as a mirror forms images the same size as objects.
It is larger for near customers, smaller for those far away.
optionWhy: A student who expects a convex mirror to magnify, as a convex lens does, picks this. A convex mirror diverges light and forms reduced images; that is why it shows a wide view of the store.

For any real object in front of a convex mirror, 1/s_i = 1/f − 1/s_o with f < 0 gives a virtual image with |s_i| < s_o, so |M| < 1: the image is always reduced, though it grows as the customer approaches.
A student who carries over the plane-mirror rule picks this. Only a plane mirror forms same-size images; a convex mirror's images are smaller than the objects.
A student who treats a convex mirror like a concave one picks this. The image of a nearer customer is larger than that of a farther one, but it is still smaller than the customer.
questions.explain: For any real object in front of a convex mirror, 1/s_i = 1/f − 1/s_o with f < 0 gives a virtual image with |s_i| < s_o, so |M| < 1: the image is always reduced, though it grows as the customer approaches.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of refraction?
options: A person sees their own face in a flat mirror on a bathroom wall.
Light spreads out after it passes through a very narrow slit in a card.
Light passes straight through a window that it strikes head-on.
A straw in a glass of water looks bent at the water's surface.
optionWhy: A student who uses refraction as another name for reflection picks this. The mirror sends light back into the air it came from; that is reflection. Refraction needs light to pass from one medium into another.

A student who confuses refraction with diffraction picks this. The light is in air on both sides of the slit, so no boundary between two media is crossed; spreading through a narrow opening is diffraction, a wave effect.

A student who thinks any light passing through a transparent material is refracted picks this. Light that strikes the glass head-on (along the normal) does not change direction, so it is transmitted without being refracted.

Refraction is a change in direction of light as it passes from one medium into another. Light from the part of the straw under water changes direction as it passes from the water into the air at the surface, so that part of the straw appears displaced and the straw looks bent where it meets the surface.
questions.explain: Refraction is a change in direction of light as it passes from one medium into another. Light from the part of the straw under water changes direction as it passes from the water into the air at the surface, so that part of the straw appears displaced and the straw looks bent where it meets the surface.

questions.q: A ray of light in water strikes the boundary with air at exactly the critical angle for that boundary. Which statement describes what happens at the boundary?
options: A refracted ray travels along the boundary, at 90° to the normal.
A refracted ray leaves along the normal, at 90° to the boundary.
All of the light reflects back, and no refracted ray exists at all.
The ray continues into the air in the direction it had in the water.
optionWhy: At the critical angle Snell's law gives n_water sin θ_critical = n_air sin θ_2 = n_air, so sin θ_2 = 1 and θ_2 = 90°: the refracted ray leaves at 90° to the normal and travels along the surface.
A student who measures angles from the surface picks this, reading 'refracts at 90°' as 90° to the boundary. The angle of refraction is measured from the normal, so 90° means along the boundary.

A student who thinks total reflection starts at the critical angle itself picks this. At exactly the critical angle a refracted ray still exists and grazes the surface; all of the light is reflected only beyond the critical angle.
A student who thinks light changes direction only on entering a material picks this. Light leaving water for air refracts away from the normal; at the critical angle it is bent all the way to 90°.
questions.explain: At the critical angle Snell's law gives n_water sin θ_critical = n_air sin θ_2 = n_air, so sin θ_2 = 1 and θ_2 = 90°: the refracted ray leaves at 90° to the normal and travels along the surface.
questions.working: n_water sin θ_critical = n_air sin θ_2 with sin θ_critical = n_air/n_water gives sin θ_2 = 1, θ_2 = 90° from the normal: the refracted ray grazes the boundary.

questions.q: The index of refraction of a certain plastic is 1.5. Which statement correctly describes what this value means?
options: Light travels 1.5 times as fast in the plastic as in a vacuum.
The plastic's mass density is 1.5 times the mass density of water.
A ray entering from air is bent to 1/1.5 of its angle of incidence.
Light travels 1.5 times as fast in a vacuum as it does in the plastic.
optionWhy: A student who treats the index as proportional to the speed picks this. The index is inversely proportional to the speed: n = c/v, so the light is slower in the plastic, and no material makes light faster than c.

A student who identifies the index with mass density picks this. The index compares speeds of light, n = c/v; it is not a ratio of densities. Olive oil, for example, is less dense than water but has a greater index.
A student who applies Snell's law to the angles themselves picks this. Snell's law relates the sines: sin θ_2 = (sin θ_1)/1.5 for a ray entering from air, and the angles are not in that ratio.
n = c/v, so n = 1.5 means c = 1.5v: light in a vacuum travels 1.5 times as fast as light in the plastic, and v = c/1.5 = 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
questions.explain: n = c/v, so n = 1.5 means c = 1.5v: light in a vacuum travels 1.5 times as fast as light in the plastic, and v = c/1.5 = 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

questions.q: A narrow beam of light traveling parallel to the principal axis, but above it, strikes a thin convex lens. Which statement describes the beam after it passes through the lens?
options: It spreads away from the axis, as if coming from the near focal point.
It crosses the principal axis at the focal point beyond the lens.
It meets the axis at 2F, two focal lengths past the lens.
It goes straight through, as it is already parallel to the axis.
optionWhy: A student who carries over the mirror rule (a convex mirror spreads light out) picks this. A convex lens is thicker in the middle and converges parallel light; spreading as if from the near focal point is what a concave (diverging) lens does.

A convex lens is a converging lens: rays arriving parallel to the principal axis are refracted so that they converge toward a common location on the transmitted (far) side of the lens, the focal point.
A student who confuses the focal point with the point 2F picks this. Parallel rays converge at the focal point, one focal length beyond the lens; 2F is twice as far away.

A student who confuses a ray parallel to the axis with the ray along the axis picks this. Only a ray along the axis (or through the center of the lens) goes straight through; a ray above the axis is bent toward the focal point.
questions.explain: A convex lens is a converging lens: rays arriving parallel to the principal axis are refracted so that they converge toward a common location on the transmitted (far) side of the lens, the focal point.

questions.q: Use the convention that s_o is positive, s_i is positive for an image on the side of the lens opposite the object and negative for an image on the same side as the object, and f is positive for a converging lens and negative for a diverging lens. A student applies the thin-lens equation to a single thin lens and a real object and finds s_i = −15 cm. What does the negative sign indicate?
options: A screen 15 cm from the lens, on the object's side, would display it.
The image is inverted, because a negative value means upside down.
The image is virtual, so no screen placed anywhere would show it.
The lens is diverging, as a converging lens forms real images.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a virtual image can be caught on a screen picks this. The negative s_i does place the image 15 cm from the lens on the object's side, but the refracted light never passes through that point; it only appears to come from there, so a screen placed there shows no image.
A student who reads the sign of s_i as the orientation picks this. The sign of s_i gives location; a virtual image formed by a single lens is upright.

In this convention a negative s_i places the image 15 cm from the lens on the same side as the object. For a single lens the refracted light leaves on the other side and only appears to come from that point, so the image is virtual: the light never meets there, and no screen position catches the image.

A student who thinks converging lenses always form real images picks this. A converging lens with the object inside the focal point also gives a negative s_i (a magnifying glass), so the sign alone does not show that the lens is diverging.
questions.explain: In this convention a negative s_i places the image 15 cm from the lens on the same side as the object. For a single lens the refracted light leaves on the other side and only appears to come from that point, so the image is virtual: the light never meets there, and no screen position catches the image.
questions.working: Convention: s_i < 0 → image 15 cm from the lens on the object's side; the refracted light only appears to diverge from there, so the image is virtual and cannot be caught on a screen. Both lens types can give s_i < 0.

questions.q: The diagram shows an object, a thin convex lens with its focal points F, and one ray from the tip of the object as it travels toward the lens. How does this ray travel after it passes through the lens?
options: Through the focal point on the right
Straight on, without changing direction
Bent outward, away from the principal axis
Out parallel to the principal axis
optionWhy: A student who thinks every ray through a converging lens goes through the far focal point picks this. That rule is for rays arriving parallel to the axis; a ray through the near focal point leaves parallel to the axis.

A student who swaps the principal-ray rules picks this. The ray that goes straight on is the one through the center of the lens; this ray meets the lens below the center, after passing through the near focal point.
A student who carries over the mirror rule (a convex mirror spreads light out) picks this. A convex lens is converging: it bends this ray back toward the axis until it leaves parallel to it.

The ray passes through the focal point on the incident side before it reaches the lens. This is one of the three principal rays: a ray through the near focal point is refracted so that it leaves parallel to the principal axis.
questions.explain: The ray passes through the focal point on the incident side before it reaches the lens. This is one of the three principal rays: a ray through the near focal point is refracted so that it leaves parallel to the principal axis.

Points labeled F are on the axis at equal distances to the left and right of the lens. An upright arrow, the object, stands on the axis at the far left, beyond the left F. Nothing is drawn to the right of the lens.

questions.q: A narrow beam of light in air strikes the flat top surface of a thick block of clear glass at an angle of incidence of 30°. Which statement describes what happens to the light?
options: Some is reflected and some enters the glass, where a small part of it is absorbed.
None of it is reflected; all of it enters the glass, which is clear rather than shiny.
All of it is reflected or all is transmitted, with the angle deciding which one.
Some is reflected and the rest crosses the block, since clear glass absorbs no light.
optionWhy: At a boundary between media with different indices of refraction, the light divides: part is reflected and part is transmitted into the glass. Glass is not perfectly transparent, so a small part of the transmitted light is absorbed as it travels through the thick block; the reflected, transmitted and absorbed parts together account for all of the incident light.

A student who thinks only shiny surfaces reflect light picks this. Clear glass reflects part of the light at its surface (about 4% at normal incidence), which is why you can see faint reflections in a window.

A student who pictures light at a boundary as going one way or the other picks this. The light divides at the surface at any angle of incidence; all-or-nothing reflection happens only in total internal reflection, which needs light traveling toward a smaller index, not from air into glass.

A student who thinks only dark materials absorb light picks this. Clear glass absorbs a small fraction of the light passing through it, more for a thicker block; a thick slab of window glass looks green when viewed through its edge.
questions.explain: At a boundary between media with different indices of refraction, the light divides: part is reflected and part is transmitted into the glass. Glass is not perfectly transparent, so a small part of the transmitted light is absorbed as it travels through the thick block; the reflected, transmitted and absorbed parts together account for all of the incident light.

questions.q: A student wants to predict whether light traveling in one transparent medium undergoes a 180° phase change when it reflects from a second transparent medium. Which information does the student need?
options: The index of refraction of the second medium, from which the light reflects
Which of the two media has the greater mass density, the first or the second
How the index of refraction of the second medium compares with that of the first
The thickness of the second medium and the wavelength of the light used
optionWhy: A student who treats the phase change as a property of the reflecting material picks this. The same material can give either result: light in air reflecting from glass changes phase, but light in diamond reflecting from glass does not. The index of the first medium is needed for the comparison.
A student who reads 'denser medium' as a medium of greater mass density picks this. The comparison is between indices of refraction: oil is less dense than water but can have the greater index.

The phase change on reflection depends on the relative indices of the two media: light reflected from a medium of greater index changes phase by 180°, and light reflected from a medium of smaller index does not. Both indices are needed to make the comparison.

A student who mixes up the phase change on reflection with the phase difference from the extra path in a film picks this. Thickness and wavelength matter for the path difference; the phase change on reflection depends only on the two indices.
questions.explain: The phase change on reflection depends on the relative indices of the two media: light reflected from a medium of greater index changes phase by 180°, and light reflected from a medium of smaller index does not. Both indices are needed to make the comparison.

questions.q: Light traveling in air passes into a block of glass at normal incidence. Which statement about the light transmitted into the glass is correct?
options: Its phase shifts by 180° at the boundary, as glass has the greater index.
Its frequency decreases in the glass, because it travels more slowly there.
Its phase is continuous across the boundary, with no 180° shift.
Its wavelength is unchanged in the glass, because its color does not change.
optionWhy: A student who applies the reflection rule to transmitted light picks this. The 180° change happens to the light reflected from the glass; the light transmitted into the glass has no phase change.
A student who links a smaller speed to a smaller frequency picks this. The frequency is set by the source and is the same in air and in glass; the smaller speed goes with a shorter wavelength, λ/n.

Refraction does not change the phase of a wave: the transmitted wave continues from the incident wave without a sudden shift. Its speed and wavelength change in the glass, but its frequency does not. A 180° phase change can happen only to the reflected light.

A student who ties each color to one fixed wavelength picks this. In the glass the light is slower at the same frequency, so its wavelength is shorter, λ/n; it has the same color again when it leaves.
questions.explain: Refraction does not change the phase of a wave: the transmitted wave continues from the incident wave without a sudden shift. Its speed and wavelength change in the glass, but its frequency does not. A 180° phase change can happen only to the reflected light.
questions.working: Refraction leaves the phase continuous (no 180° shift); f is unchanged, v = c/n and λ_n = λ/n decrease.

questions.q: Which observation is one that classical physics could not explain and that helped lead to the development of quantum theory?
options: How the intensity of the radiation emitted by a hot, glowing object varies with wavelength
The pattern of bright and dark bands formed by light passing through two narrow slits
The curved path followed by a beam of electrons as it moves through a magnetic field
The random, jittery motion of pollen grains suspended in a drop of water under a microscope
optionWhy: Classical physics could not account for the way the intensity of blackbody radiation is distributed over wavelengths; explaining it was one of the problems that led to quantum theory, along with atomic spectra and the photoelectric effect.

A student who links the double-slit experiment with quantum physics picks this. The interference pattern of light is explained by the classical wave model; it was the evidence, in Young's experiment, that light behaves as a wave.

A student who thinks anything involving electrons needs quantum theory picks this. The curved path of an electron beam many centimeters across is explained by the classical magnetic force on a moving charge.
A student who thinks anything microscopic is quantum picks this. The jittery motion of pollen grains comes from collisions with water molecules and is explained by classical physics.
questions.explain: Classical physics could not account for the way the intensity of blackbody radiation is distributed over wavelengths; explaining it was one of the problems that led to quantum theory, along with atomic spectra and the photoelectric effect.

questions.q: Which statement about electrons is consistent with quantum theory?
options: They are tiny particles, and only light, not matter, can form an interference pattern.
They are particles moving along wavy paths, and this wiggling is what makes them wave-like.
They are more wave-like the faster they move, as their wavelength grows with speed.
Each is detected at a single point, yet an electron beam can form an interference pattern.
optionWhy: A student who thinks only light can behave as a wave picks this. Electron beams produce interference patterns when they pass through two slits or a crystal, which shows that electrons have wave properties.
A student who pictures the wave as a wiggling path picks this. Wave behavior shows up as interference and diffraction patterns, not as a sideways wiggle in the electron's path.
A student who reads λ = h/p as a direct relationship picks this. The de Broglie wavelength decreases as the momentum increases, so faster electrons have shorter wavelengths.

In quantum theory fundamental particles such as electrons show both particle-like behavior (each electron is detected at one point) and wave-like behavior (a beam of electrons produces interference and diffraction patterns).
questions.explain: In quantum theory fundamental particles such as electrons show both particle-like behavior (each electron is detected at one point) and wave-like behavior (a beam of electrons produces interference and diffraction patterns).

questions.q: Which statement about the wave model and the photon model of light is correct?
options: The photon model replaced the wave model, which experiments showed to be wrong.
The two combine: photons are particles traveling along wave-shaped paths.
Each model explains some observations of light, so both models are needed.
The wave model explains energy transfer; photons explain double-slit bands.
optionWhy: A student who thinks newer models overturn older ones picks this. The wave model still correctly explains interference and diffraction; the photon model adds what the wave model cannot explain.
A student who pictures the wave as a wiggling path picks this. A photon in empty space travels in a straight line; light's wave behavior shows up in interference patterns, not in the shape of a path.

Light can be modeled both as a wave and as discrete photons. The wave model explains interference and diffraction; the photon model explains observations in which light delivers energy in discrete amounts. Both are needed.

A student who thinks the double-slit pattern is evidence for photons picks this. The bright and dark bands of a double slit are explained by the wave model; photons are needed to explain energy delivered in discrete amounts.
